articles.text: Crow’s contact with PG&E line causes 24,000 buildings to lose power A crow came in contact with and damaged Pacific Gas and Electric (PG&E) equipment on the morning of August 25, causing a temporary outage that affected 24,000 customers in Alameda County. The outage occurred on Thursday morning at 11 a.m. and affected residents and business owners in the Oakland Hills, Montclair, Piedmont, Oakland, and Mills College. Traffic lights were out at the main intersection in Piedmont at Oakland and Grand Avenues. “Several intersections were without power affecting traffic signals. Portable stop signs were brought out to control traffic, and police staff monitored intersections for any issues,” confirmed Piedmont Police Department Commander Lisa Douglas. “The police department building experienced a brief power outage, but generators provided emergency power. Emergency dispatchers answered several calls inquiring about the power outage. We would like to remind the public that we have one dispatcher on duty who answers both 911 and non-emergency calls. In most circumstances, we have no information about the source or duration of the power outage,” she added. The Piedmont Fire Department had minimal impact from the power outage, confirmed Fire Chief Dave Brannigan. “We got one call for a false fire alarm likely triggered by the outage but no other calls. Our station has a generator, so we were able to receive and respond if needed,” he said. articles.text: Are cattle chutes in the future for residents? The following letter was sent to the Piedmont City Council. Editor: I am a long-time resident of the Piedmont Manor neighborhood on York Drive. I want to express my deep concerns about the new sidewalk and curbs being installed at Holly Place and Manor Drive. The selected design decision was clearly made without regard to the function of sidewalks and streets in this pedestrian-friendly and bikefriendly neighborhood. There is clearly no citywide consistency in design standards, and I urge you to direct Public Works to install infrastructure that meets the needs of users. My objections to the partially completed concrete infrastructure are: • Safety is degraded • Pedestrian flow is reduced • Green space is reduced Safety degradation The previous design was pedestrian-friendly, with wide and minimally-sloped transitions from sidewalk to street. The new infrastructure requires almost a 90-degree turn by each pedestrian, and only one person at a time, almost like cattle being slotted into a narrow chute. People do not move in this manner, and most will step up on the new curb, go across the new concrete and down the other step into the deeply-guttered street. This movement involving new hazards is almost required by the current design. Pedestrian flow degradation Holly Place and the public cutthrough from Holly to Ricardo Avenue is a conduit for hundreds of students headed to Beach School, Piedmont Middle School, and Piedmont High School every day. The movement of young students with parents toward Beach School is made in groups, and the new design squeezes the flow into a single-file, one-way movement. This is not feasible for parent and children, or groups with bikes, scooters, wheelchairs or strollers. The natural work-around will be to use the street for group movement, which will be worse than the current situation. Green space reduction The city will be moving against its own environmental policies by turning green space between the sidewalk and street into concrete. This location is best served with wide, minimally-sloped transitions from sidewalk to street. I see many Piedmont sidewalks with date stamps from the 1920s and 1930s. Please do not move forward with a design that degrades safety, pedestrian flow and green space for the next 100 years. –Ellen Smith 460 Boulevard Way, Oakland, CA 94610 Phone: 652-2051 • email: news@piedmontpost.org Publisher & Editor: Gray Cathrall City Editor: Allyson Aleksey PRODUCTION MANAGER Victor Cheng REPORTERS Jay Russell Ed Gilligan Will Becker (intern) SCHOOLS Ada Cliff SPORTS Jonathan Comeaux B. articles.text: Sara Paul of Watch Duty opens series on September 7 Sara Paul of Watch Duty will be the guest speaker for Connect’s speaker series on September 7. The Piedmont League of Women Voters (LWV) and Piedmont Connect are co-hosting a climate speaker series, beginning with guest speaker Sara Paul from Watch Duty. Her talk will be on Wednesday, September 7 at 4 p.m. The speaker series will continue through May 2023. Watch Duty launched in August 2021 as a smartphone application and interactive map that shows where wildfires are burning across the state in realtime with information gathered from a variety of channels and agencies. Watch Duty covered Sonoma, Napa and Lake counties in its inception, and has since expanded to include all 58 counties in California. Paul manages Sonoma County Fire Updates for the app and will speak on wildfire mitigation at next week’s Zoom event. “Watch Duty fills an important gap as a source of reliable fire information provided in a timely manner,” said Paul. “Our target audience is anyone living in fire country in California. In 2022, that’s all of us.” The Watch Duty team monitors a network of sources to bring information directly to the user. Among its trusted channels are flight patterns of California Department of Forestry and Fire Protection (CAL FIRE), the statewide network of ALERT wildfire camera, and satellite data. The speaker series aims to educate constituents on a range of important topics with a focus on environmentalism and sustainability. Paul’s presentation will be followed by a question-and-answer session. Sign up for the speaker series at https://lwvpiedmont.org/content.aspx?page_id=4002&club_ id=601389&item_id=1765943. The event begins at 4 p.m. Registration is free and open to all. The program will be recorded and can be watched after the fact on LWV’s YouTube channel. articles.text: The city of Piedmont held a final community workshop on its draft housing element, published on April 8 this year, prior to City Council review. The hybrid informational session was held in City Hall and on Zoom on August 18. City Administrator Sara Lillevand and Planning Director Kevin Jackson facilitated the meeting. Piedmont is a member of the Association of Bay Area Governments (ABAG), which allocates housing mandates to each jurisdiction based on multifaceted methodology. Piedmont did raise concerns numerous times during ABAG’s housing mandate process with questions as to where the methodology was headed, Lillevand explained. This cycle’s methodology largely considered access to opportunity and proximity to jobs - Piedmont is considered a “high resource area” and is close to transit hubs, which increased its allotted regional housing needs allocation (RHNA). “All of Piedmont is considered a high resource area, with [access] to great schools, city services and amenities which contribute to positive outcomes - and as a result, Piedmont was allocated more units [this cycle],” Lillevand said. Proximity to jobs across the Bay Area was also a factor ABAG considered when handing Piedmont a total of 587 low to moderate income units. Lillevand said she considered where city and school employees fall under the income based allocation, and found that nearly 80% of city workforce falls under the low-income category, with less than $110,000 of household income. Piedmont is not alone in this challenge, Lillevand said - Albany, Emeryville, Orinda, Sausalito, Tiburon, and more cities that fall under ABAG’s mandate process all saw dramatic increases in their RHNA. “If the city is not in compliance with state housing law, it will be ineligible to receive grants and loan programs, and will be unable to issue building permits, conditional use permits and design review permits,” Jackson explained. “[Incompliance] leaves the city vulnerable to costly litigation from housing rights organizations, developers and HCD.” “If the city is not in compliance, it will only have one year

articles.text: A volleyball subcommittee, consisting of Recreation Commissioners Dick Carter, Lisa Gardner, and Aamir Virani, conducted a citywide survey to gauge interest in beach volleyball courts in town. Although the survey found that there is interest in the sport, funding and space constraints have halted the project. There are no dedicated outdoor volleyball or beach volleyball courts in Piedmont. A group of Piedmont parents, including Kim DeYoung, Kiel Murray, and Zoa Town, advocated creating beach volleyball courts in town, with the primary focus of finding a practice and competition space for a future Piedmont High School girls’ beach volleyball team. The Recreation Department offers recreational volleyball opportunities for girls and boys aged 7 to 18 during the fall, spring, and summer, but none for those over 18. Based on the group’s strong interest in beach volleyball, the Recreation Commission formed a volleyball subcommittee in January. “The advocates got up to speed really fast and figured out a way to move the ball forward,” said Virani. “[Based on a citywide survey] we found that there is community interest in beach volleyball and the development of courts.” Virani added that the survey was informal, although there were 272 responses. The subcommittee then met over six months to discuss survey findings and next steps. “It was interesting to work on this project, with lots of discussion. We tried to get as much information as we could when we put this together,” Virani said. The subcommittee considered that city space is at a premium and found concerns regarding adding programming to “already strained resources from the perspectives of facility sharing, historical usage, adaptability of facilities, and noise impacts,” according to the survey results report. “When the master plans for city parks are revisited, at that time, the city, park commission and recreation commission should work together, along with the recreation department, to consider beach volleyball courts at that time,” Virani said. City parks master plans are revisited when funding allows, with no set date at this time. “This is disappointing, but not entirely surprising,” Town said to commissioners at an August 17 meeting. “We are focused on working with PUSD to get the facility we need. It’s slow, it’s like hitting a heavy volleyball through the wind, but it’s moving forward.” DeYoung echoed Town’s sentiments. “I ask for advocacy and support,” she told commissioners. “It’s hard being parents of high school students. I know the high school is trying to identify more athletic opportunities for female athletes. Beach volleyball was the number one sport of interest [for female students].”
articles.title: City plan for adult beach volleyball halted

articles.text: The Piedmont Recreation Commission established an Older Adult Programming Subcommittee at an August 17 meeting. Recreation Supervisor Eva Phalen will serve as staff lead for the subcommittee. “We heard from the community that there is increased interest in more [older adult] programming,” Phalen said. “The goal is to figure out what people are looking for and in what structure.” Some classes and meetups have been successful, Phalen added, like Walking on Wednesday, organized by Recreation Commissioner Vice Chair Dick Carter. “I’m excited about this and have lots of ideas,” Phalen said, and added that the department is interested in opening up programming to individuals beyond Piedmont. “This has been an area of interest of mine for some time,” Carter said, who wrote a proposed program in 2018 to address older adult recreational programming. “There are about 2,350 people over the age of 65 in Piedmont, according to the census. That’s up from about 1,600 in 2010, so our population is growing older.” Walking on Wednesday and an established reading group have been successful. Over 140 people have signed up for Walking on Wednesday, with an average of 30-35 per week. Carter and commissioner Lisa Gardener were the first to volunteer to be on the subcommittee.

articles.text: Anne Valva began her tenure as Beach School Principal one week ago after being confirmed by the Piedmont School Board on August 24. Valva’s first year as a principal follows 30 years of experience in education. She has been at Beach since 2013 as a fifth grade teacher and Math Intervention Specialist. “My first few days as principal have been so much fun,” said Valva. “The students and families have been so welcoming and the teachers are very supportive. I am constantly learning.” The top position at Beach opened when Michael Corritone committed to a principal position in Walnut Creek on August 1, just nine days before Piedmont’s school year began. The school district quickly posted the job on Edjoin to field applicants. After two rounds of interviews Valva was named the top choice. “The main reason I applied for the job is that I want to continue the great work the teachers, staff and students do at Beach School every day,” Valva explained. Valva’s career path began to finding her home at Beach School. After teaching 5th grade at Beach for four years she became the school’s Math Intervention Specialist, a role she has enjoyed from 2017 until the first week of this year. “She comes highly recommended from fellow staff and families and I look forward to watching her build on an already thriving school community,” said Piedmont Interim Superintendent, Dr. Donald Evans. Valva has served Beach in many roles that will serve her well as Principal, including being a member of the school’s Leadership and Response to Intervention Teams. She has worked at the elementary and District-levels analyzing and interpreting assessment data and passing on the information to fellow teachers to more successfully implement classroom curriculum. articles.text: Piedmont Education Foundation (PEF) presented a check for $3,350,402 to the Piedmont School Board on August 24. The funds represent the culmination of fundraising campaigns from last year (2021-2022) principally through the Giving Campaign. “We are humbled by the generosity of our community,” said Amelie Kappes, Chair of the Foundation’s board. “Once again, Piedmont has shown its commitment to our schools and our students.” A total of 1,216 families contributed to the 2021-2022 Giving Campaign with an average gift of $3,075. The grant provides 42,000 hours of instructional and student support and represents an $2,316,000 in teacher salaries, $925,000 in student support staff, and $109,000 in teacher professional development, instructional technology, and classroom supplies. The grant also includes funding for mental health counseling, tutoring, and libraries. For more details, visit piedmontedfoundation.org/our-impact/grantsschool-support/. “We are thankful for the hard work of our Giving Campaign chairs, Colleen Allan and Christine Wente von Metzsch, and to the whole Giving Campaign team for their record-breaking success,” said Heather Frank, PEF Executive Director. “They really brought our community together to share the importance of giving to our schools.” Megan Pillsbury, the School Photo by Jane Violich Giving Campaign Chairs: Dana Murray (left), Katie Sharafi, and Julia Ruthven. articles.text: Are your kids ready for school? With 2022 back-to-school already upon us, our children are experiencing a wide range of individual experiences. Some variability is due to differences in educational settings and pandemic related factors. But not all. What constitutes “school readiness”? A wide body of research has examined the neurodevelopmental elements required for a child to be ready for school. Is it certain pre-academic skills? Is it social aptitude? Emotional maturity? Review of the literature shows that a child’s ability in one kindergarten readiness area prior to school entry is predictive of continued success in that same academic area. For example, a child’s preschool alphabet and phonics skill level is predictive of their reading level later on. But is there an indicator that predicts skill acquisition both within and across domains? For example, we know that foundational pre-math skills at preschool predicts a child’s ability in that subject, but do preschool math skills correlate with success in any other academic or social domains? Analysis of children’s assessment data taken before kindergarten entry, and again in the first, third and fifth grades, reveal that language ability has the most wide-reaching effects on school readiness and ongoing academic success. That is, researchers found that the language skills a child exhibited before entering school predicted not only that child’s school-aged level of communication skills, but also their overall levels in reading, writing, math and to some extent social skills. Researchers hypothesize that language skills are correlated with so many other key areas, because language serves as a set of tools that helps children acquire other skills. For example, we use our language comprehension to understand numeracy and vocabulary concepts, which leads to stronger math and reading skills. We also use our expressive abilities to connect with others and explain our thinking, which may be why stronger language skills support our social skills. So, what does it actually mean to be ready for school? Perhaps it means language! For some at-risk children, this could mean we focus on prevention. For some children with speech and language delays, this could mean we focus on treatment. And for most children this could mean we focus on language enrichment. Katie Pengilly is a Speech and Language Pathologist, and the owner of SPEECH Inc., a pediatric private practice specializing in speech, language, reading and writing. I served as Havens’ Parent Club President, on the LCAP Committee, Superintendent Community Advisory Committee, and Wellness Center Committee, to name a few. As a member of PUSD’s Board of Education, my priorities would be to ensure PUSD has the leadership and resources to provide students an excellent, well-rounded academic experience, including the hiring of a superintendent aligned in our goals, and attracting and retaining well-qualified, diverse, engaged educators. This will allow PUSD to truly equip students with the essential critical-thinking, STEAM, and language arts skills needed to succeed at the universities and in the careers of their choosing. I have attended California public schools my entire life, culminating in degrees from Cal Berkeley and UCSD. Piedmont schools are the foundation of our community, yet the past three years have been divisive. To move forward we must engage in meaningful community dialogue, be pragmatic and creative, ensure all stakeholders are engaged in our decision-making processes, and always put students first. Shirley Hooi COVID-related online learning has forced PUSD students to endure an unprecedented period of educational losses and mental stress. Now is a crucial period to help our students get back on track. I believe that parent, student and community member involvement in school board decisions is critical. Their opinions should be considered in the selection of the superintendent, along with issues regarding school curriculum and teacher retention/recruitment. As a product of the Oakland Unified School District, PUSD was regarded as the epitome of an exceptional public school education. Families strived to move to Piedmont to raise their children in a community in which a public school education was comparable to the local private schools. Unfortunately, this has changed, and PUSD continues to lose students to local private schools every year. My immigrant parents instilled in their children the belief of education and hard work as a path out of poverty. Now as a PUSD parent, it is my role to instill the same beliefs upon my children. If you support this philosophy, now is the time for me to be your voice on the school board. Get Involved: www.shirleyhooi.com.

articles.text: Betsy Andersen, incumbent My priorities on the Piedmont City Council have been community health and safety, financial stability, and strong city-school relations. During my time on Council, we have renovated Hampton Park and the Corey Reich Tennis Center, invested $3.75M for future pension needs, facilitated in-town COVID-19 testing, allocated funds to modernize police and fire dispatch, and maintained a balanced budget. Currently, we are rebuilding the city-owned Piedmont Community Pool, thanks to voter-approved Measure UU. As a lifelong resident, I appreciate the challenges and opportunities as we develop strategies to meet our climate action goals, address the state housing crisis, and replace aging infrastructure. Prior to serving on Council, I volunteered on the Public Safety Committee to promote emergency preparedness and chaired the Recreation Commission with a focus on improving recreational facilities and opportunities for all ages. I attended Piedmont public schools, majored in Public Policy at Duke, earned my law degree from UCLA, and practiced law for nearly two decades. My husband, Robert, and I raised our daughters here, Jane (PHS ’18) and Ellie (PHS ’21). If re-elected, I will continue to listen thoughtfully to all voices as we work together to strengthen the community we call home. Jennifer Long, incumbent I am running for City Council to serve our beautiful community and maintain its greatness as it grows and evolves. With an impending pool build, critical infrastructure repair (and or replacement) and housing development, Piedmont is poised to be a city with the future in mind. In these unprecedented times, our city needs leaders who understand the interests of our citizens

articles.text: Wearing purple and white as Piedmont High’s No. 1 singles starter on the tennis team this coming fall season, Tanya Kononova will be a new face on the team. She never could have imagined coming to California as a high school student prior to February 24, the day Russia invaded her native country of Ukraine. She arrived in Piedmont with her mother just one month ago on July 22 from Odesa, a city on the southern shore of Ukraine. Kononova, a junior at PHS, showed up one week later at a tennis clinic being run by varsity coach Jim Landes, and instantly impressed him. “It was the week I had a warm-up clinic for high school girls. I told her to come the next day and she showed up to the clinics every day. The first time she hit, right then and there I knew she was a very good player. It was also a good time for her to meet some people,” said Landes. Having to leave your country is an unimaginable experience. Kononova and her mother, Olga Charugina, packed what they could into two suitcases and drove to the border of Moldova three weeks after the Russians invaded. Her father is still in Ukraine as men under the age of 60-years old were required to stay and help in Ukraine’s war with Russia. To enter Moldova, Tanya and her mother had to wait at the border for 13 hours. “It was very scary to be leaving the Ukraine because we were afraid of being hit by bombs. There were so many people waiting at the border trying to get out,” said Kononova, They stayed in Moldova with relatives for two months but after the building of the town administration was targeted by Russian artillery, they decided to flee to Bulgaria, where they would stay from May through July. It would be their last stop before flying to the U.S. “We had no relatives there [in Bulgaria]. We had a place where we lived – my mother, my grandfather and grandmother and me. My grandparents are still in Bulgaria now,” said Kononova. When initially leaving Odesa, she and her family were forced to quickly throw together their belongings because of fear that the Russians would siege the city. “The first time we left, we hurried to pack in one night because everybody was afraid that the Russians would eventually take Odesa, so we left very quickly. We basically narrowed things down to what would fit in two suitcases,” said Kononova. There was a moment when Tanya traveled back to her home in Odesa for a week in order to grab more belongings. She and her friend went to a mall when a rocket struck a building close by. In a recent interview, Kononova details the emotions she experienced. “When we were leaving for Moldova, I didn’t feel that much. But we had to come back to Odesa for a week and that’s where it really hit me. I went shopping with a friend and when we were in a store, we were told to go to a shelter because they detected a missile, but we paid no attention. Then we heard an explosion which felt like it was right next to us. There were four more explosions, and it was one of the days they bombed one of the residential areas in Odesa. I couldn’t sleep that night and kept moving my bed away from the window. That’s when we understood that we needed to leave,” she explained. Since then, Kononova’s family and friends have been widespread, while some are still residing in Odesa. Her best friend is now living in London, while other friends have scattered around Europe. Tanya and her mother, meanwhile, moved into her uncle’s home in Piedmont. “Some people moved entire families; some moved just their kids. I’m still in touch with all of my friends. One of my friends was able to fly into Bulgaria to visit me,” said Kononova. Now enrolled in high school as a junior and on the school tennis team, she is playing tennis for the first time since February. “She is playing with my racket,” said PHS coach Jim Landes with a wide smile. Piedmont High School junior Tanya Kononova, the school’s No. 1 singles starter on the tennis team, discusses her experience as a Ukrainian refugee. Tanya began playing tennis when she was six years old and continued at the club level through her teenage years. She instantly made friends with her Piedmont teammates, though the concept of playing on a team is new to her. Tennis is, after all, an individual sport. “It’s completely different from the places where I was before. But it’s a nice place and it feels like you are safe here. The people are quite happy to see you… Playing on the team definitely makes me feel like someone stands for me. You’re not alone and it’s less stressful. “It’s also more fun,” Kononova added. Coach Landes adds that the team has already taken well to her. “I think all the teammates really like her. It’s a new school for her, so having this activity helps her meet people and bond with them. If she wasn’t a tennis player and just went to this new school without being an athlete, I think it would be much more difficult. She already knows a bunch of girls,” said Landes. Tanya already has set a goal for this season, and it’s an ambitious one. “I don’t want to lose a single match,” said Kononova with a smile. The Post welcomes Tanya and her mother to Piedmont and thanks Tanya for her courage in being willing to describe her experiences of the past six months. articles.text: Head coaches switch; Krumins to take lead, Savage to assist Piedmont’s defending WACC Championship boys’ water polo team returns for the fall season, but with a couple of changes. John Savage has stepped down as head coach entering his 10th year at the helm in favor of assistant coach Rik Krumins. Savage will continue as the varsity assistant and be the head coach of the junior varsity team for at least the 2022 season. The two have coached together for six years, share a mutual philosophy. The change in title will allow Krumins to coach his son, Peter Krumins, a junior. He was the Post’s Sophomore of the Year in 2022.. “We’ve decided that we’ll be co-head coaches, essentially, and that’s been the dynamic for a while. With water polo, only one coach is allowed to stand during games, so he’ll be the one standing and yelling. So, he can yell at his son,” added Savage with a laugh. articles.text: Asian Art Museum of San Francisco is exhibiting Filipino artist Carlos Villa’s work now through October 24. San Francisco-born Villa was a groundbreaking, 20th century modern artist whose work explores the meaning of cultural diversity in America. The exhibition, entitled Carlos Villa: Worlds in Collision, focuses mainly on the artist’s drawings, mixed-media painting, and constructions from the 1970s up until his death in 2013. Villa experimented with techniques of Western painting with materials found in non-Western art; the juxtaposition is most notably in the 1970s. The exhibition is a joint effort by the Asian Art Museum and San Francisco Art Institute (SFAI). Visit https://exhibitions. asianart.org/exhibitions/carlos-villa-worlds-in-collision/ to Artist Carlos Villa learn more.

articles.text: The Chamber Music Society of San Francisco, now celebrating its 10th anniversary, returns to Piedmont for a concert on Saturday, September 17 at 7:30 p.m. at Piedmont Center for the Arts. Founding members Natasha Makhijani, Jory Fankuchen, Samsun van Loon, and Clio Tilton will perform a program to include Beethoven’s String Quartet in A minor, op. 132, Mozart’s “Dissonance” String Quartet in C Major, K465, and Caroline Shaw’s “Valencia”. For tickets click on: https://bit. ly/3TpKMUZ. Beethoven’s opus 132 string quartet is from his collection of “late” quartets, written in the final years of his life. In these works, Beethoven turned inward, leaving us with some of his most exquisite and transcendental music. The Chamber Music Society of San Francisco opens its 10th anniversary season with a return to Op. 132, the masterpiece that brought these fine musicians together a decade ago. The Chamber Music Society of San Francisco is dedicated to bringing chamber music masterworks to diverse audiences. CMS of SF is passionate about concertizing in intimate settings, creatNatasha Makhijani (left), Jory Fankuchen, Samsun van Loon, and Clio Tilton comprise the principal quartet of Chamber Music Society of San Francisco. ing close connections between performers and listeners, and cultivating a relationship between music and audiences that extends far beyond the perimeter of the concert hall. Drawing listeners into the lives of the composers and the world of the music, CMS of SF concerts are a favorite destination for both chamber music lovers and those new to the genre. Members of CMS of SF can be heard performing with the San Francisco Symphony, SF Opera, SF Ballet, the San Francisco and New Century Chamber Orchestras, American Bach Soloists, the Oakland Symphony and many others. Founding members Natasha Makhijani, Jory Fankuchen, Samsun van Loon, and Clio Tilton came together through their mutual love of the late Beethoven String Quartets. articles.text: American Conservatory Theatre (ACT) presents Passengers onstage at the Geary Theatre in San Francisco beginning September 15. The production will run through October 9. The road to Carnegie Hall; the road to perdition Every composition was modern. I must admit that I am not always enthusiastic about contemporary music. Too many violinists these days emphasize the ugly. Flanagan always emphasizes the beautiful. And that’s the way it was from beginning to end. With playing like this, his success at Carnegie Hall is almost assured. The road to perdition An article in the Post last week presented the case for teaching music to all students. It was in the Back to Schools section on page 12 and entitled “the importance of music for students”. What I write here is a follow-up to those beautiful words. This is one teacher’s opinion on why all schools should teach music. The ancient Greeks had no problem integrating music and athletics. They even included mathematics and logic in the mix. If the ancient Greeks could do it, we can also. But our educational system is losing ground rapidly. What is the stumbling block? There is a huge difference between teachers and educators. Teachers do the teaching. Educators are not teachers. Educators must relinquish the territory they stake out. Will they be able to do it? Probably not. Therefore, the general public needs to become aware of the benefits of integrating music with other subjects and to re-educate our educators. Get them out of their offices and onto the front lines. Every kid needs to be in a music education class. They need to sing every day in elementary school. When I was teaching in San Francisco schools, I went to every classroom every week. One year I had 1200 students. We sang, learned to read music, played recorders, and knew every instrument of the orchestra. It is generally acknowledged that we are experiencing more problems all the time. Music is an acknowledged antidote. We must initiate the change ASAP. Get involved and speak up. articles.text: The Oakland Museum of California is celebrating Edith Heath, designer and founder of Heath Ceramics, in a display on view through October 30. Edith Heath: A Life in Clay showcases the legacy of the artist with over 50 pieces of ceramics, clay samples, photographs, and personal memorabilia on display. A documentary video is shown inside the museum as well. The new exhibition introduces visitors to the artists’ career, which was deeply expressive of California’s land and lifestyle. Heath, who died in 2005, focused on creating dependable and long-lasting products for the home, with a focus on sustainability. A Life in Clay is organized by OMCA Curator of Photography Drew Johnson, and guest curator Jennifer Volland. “Edith Heath transformed our notion of ‘good design’ pioneering a new aesthetic of natural, stylish yet functional products made from local materials and designed to endure,” said Johnson. “As an icon of quintessential California design who lived and worked in Sausalito and San Francisco, OMCA is excited to share the extraordinary story of Heath’s life and legacy.” The exhibit examines Heath’s technical experimentations with native California clays and glaze formulas. Her love of natural landscapes shaped the quality of her design and inspired her to seek clays from California rather than what was traditionally used for dinnerware. “What began as a rebellion against imported white clay more than fifty years ago is now a modern-day classic,” said Volland, who has researched the artist since 2014 and served as an essayist for the book Edith Heath: Philosophies. To learn more about the exhibition, and to purchase tickets, visit www.museumca.org. Photo by Christina Cueto A collection at Oakland Museum of California showcases Edith Heath’s ceramics.

articles.text: Elizabeth Banks and Russell Crowe in The Next Three Days. The Next Three Days is, in some ways, similar to the decidedly harrowing Unstoppable. While any comparison may seem a stretch, both films are polished B-movies with A-list actors. This represents an encouraging change. B-movies have long been the repository of second-tier talent as well as writing that lacks, well, complexity. But thankfully, this genre has experienced a renaissance of sorts over the last decade. B-movies represent, increasingly, raw and edgy filmmaking. Unlike Unstoppable, which quickly gets up to speed, The Next Three Days involves a long and complex setup. John Brennan (Russell Crowe), a local college teacher in Pittsburg, is living a nightmare. His wife, Lara (Elizabeth Banks), has been tried and convicted and recently sentenced to 20 years in prison for murder. Two years have passed since the crime. He is raising his son, with the help of his parents and trying to understand how he and his wife might ever wake up from this debilitating horror. A plan begins to take shape in John’s mind. The only alternative, he concludes, is to break Lara out of an impenetrable maximum security prison. The question is: how? Soon the wall in his dining room is filled with maps, bold notes regarding passports, escape routes, locations, times, and elaborate strategies. The wall becomes the nexus of the film and, as it fills, the tension builds. This is high risk, high gain planning and seems all but impossible from every angle. Not to forget that John is a teacher of literature and clearly unprepared to cobble together a Quixotic escape (actually, there is a nice scene where he is teaching Don Quixote to his students, something about belief in virtue is more important than virtue itself). Knowing that John is an amateur adds hugely to the sense of foreboding that gives this thriller its impetus. There is not one moment when the conclusion is foregone. This will not have a right ending. How could it? John will end up in jail along with his wife and his parents will then have to raise his son. What’s wonderful about top drawer B-movies – this one was written and directed by the highly acclaimed Paul Haggis (“Crash,” “Million Dollar Baby,” “Letters from Iwo Jima”) – is that they are focused on solving an external problem. With solid actors such as Crowe and Banks delivering exceptional performances, the entertainment payoff can be gripping. As it is in The Next Three Days. The Next Three Days. articles.text: Papa: Hemingway in Cuba was the first film shot on location in Cuba since 1959, the year that Fidel Castro came to power. The scenery is beyond beautiful, a rainbow of colors, topaz waters and classic cars. As well, many of the interior shots are actually filmed in Hemingway’s Finca Vigia, located in Havana and now a lovingly cared for museum, testimony to the Nobel and Pulitzer Prize-winning author’s prodigious talent and extraordinary life. But the promise of this film, which is never fulfilled, resides in the fact that it takes place in the late 50s (on the cusp of the Cuban revolution) when Hemingway is approaching his 59th birthday. He receives a letter from a young Miami Globe reporter, Ed Myers (Giovanni Ribisi), who shares with the aging writer how much his prose meant to him as a young person who had been abandoned by his father during the depression and grew up in a Catholic orphanage. He later went on to become a journalist and war correspondent. Not unlike Hemingway. To Myers’ surprise – initially disbelief – Hemingway calls him and thanks him for the letter and invites him to come to Cuba and go fishing. While sitting on a beach with Hemingway’s fourth wife, Mary, he tells them that he has never had a family. Hemingway (who insists on being called “Papa”) says that he and Mary will be his family. It is a moment that the young journalist could only have imagined; yet, there he is, sitting on an idyllic beach with the man who had previously only gazed back at him from a book’s dust jacket and wrote words that made all the difference. What Myers could not fully comprehend – how could he? He gazed at Hemingway through a worshipful prism – was that the renowned writer was also a mean, cruel drunk, a verbally abusive husband, and increasingly paranoid (he was convinced the F.B.I. was tailing him). He was also a man in decline. And it is that reality that is sadly missing in this film. The scaffolding of Hemingway’s life was language. Words mattered and he wrote them sparingly and beautifully. Again and again. This film needs long moments of exposition, such as discussions while sitting at dinner tables or bars or on a sunswept beach. It begs for reflection. Hemingway grappled with the reality that he was no longer the man he remembered. And he seems powerless to reframe his life, to find a path into old age that he could embrace, absent the distortions created by too much booze. Instead he sank into depression, dwelled in dark corners of regret and anger and loss and contemplated suicide seemingly daily. (He committed suicide 18 months after leaving Cuba). In one scene he puts the barrel of a gun into his mouth. This was not the man that Myers thought he was going to visit. But this was Hemingway as he approached 60. And yet the film seems unable to risk more than dwelling on Hemingway’s surface torment, absent what is behind it. Hence he says things like, “The only value we have as human beings are the risks we’re willing to take.” What does that truly mean? What was he saying about life and about himself? Clearly, the risk Hemingway was unwilling to take was that of growing old. Which may take more courage than stepping into a bullring with only a ceremonial cape and sword. Papa: Hemingway in Cuba could have been a revelation, an intimate look at the man and all of his imperfections, a man tormented by demons that formed a crucible of memories tempered by regret for all that had passed and couldn’t be changed. To my surprise, there is no mention of one of his finest and most iconic works, the elegant and beautifully written, The Old Man and the Sea – a book, a metaphor, triumphant and painful. It was his last major novel. Papa: Hemingway in Cuba. Directed by Bob Yari. Starring Adrian Sparks, Giovanni Rib, Joely Richardson. 1 hr., 49 min. Rated R. Released in 2016. Now streaming on VUDU/Prime/peacock.

articles.text: Bill Campbell and Alan Arkin in The Rocketeer. The Rocketeer, based on the graphic novel written by Dave Stevens, should appeal to a whole new generation of kids. Sure, it’s retro, set in 1942, and carried with it the hope that it would be the beginning of a superhero franchise. Alas, for reasons that remain inexplicable, it failed to find an audience, and never caught the imagination of those kids for which it was intended. Hence, no Rocketeer II. But, after a quarter of a century since its release, strangely, after a bevy of superhero movies, its special effects and energetic story can seem fresh and compelling, even with the absence of CGI, to which kids have grown so accustomed. Set in Los Angeles. The year is 1938. The film opens with Cliff Secord (Billy Campbell), a test pilot and barnstormer, finds in his crashed bi-plane a strange looking dual rocket pack with a leather harness. He takes it to his favorite mechanic, Peevy Peabody (Alan Arkin), asking him what he can make of it. It’s only later that Cliff comes to realize that the pack was stolen from Howard Hughes (Terry O’ Quinn) by a gang of thieves (who had hidden the pack in Billy’s plane to begin with) who are led by one gangster-type named Eddie Valentine (Paul Sorvino). Predictably, not only does the U.S. government want the package, but is also being sought after by a cohort of nefarious Nazis who immediately see the potential in creating an army of rocket men using the package as a weapon to take over the U.S. Of course, Cliff and Peevy figure out how to tweak the rockets, and Cliff soon finds himself going vertical, launched into the sky. It’s a rush. And thus is born what became known as the Rocketeer. Unfortunately, the baddies (the thieves and the Nazis) hear that Cliff found the package and so begin the chase to get it back. There’s even a big thug wearing a rubber mask who works for Valentine. And there’s an exciting battle between Cliff and the Nazis on top of a zeppelin. Not surprisingly, Cliff has a gorgeous girlfriend, Jenny Blake (Jennifer Connelly), who wants to become a movie star in a film with a third-rate actor, Neville Sinclair (Timothy Dalton) who also has some designs on the rockets. However, Jenny helps cliff avoid those who are desperate to get their hands on the rockets. Even Sinclair. There are lots of special effects and excitement, car chases and gunfights. There is an Indiana Jones quality to the movie, an adventure film to this day that has stood the test of time. I have a feeling that The Rocketeer, a film reminiscent of the once popular Saturday matinees, will appeal to kids of all ages and stands up well even today. The Rocketeer. Directed by Joe Johnson. Starring Bill Campbell, Jennifer Connelly and Timothy Dalton. 1 hr., 49 min. Rated PG. Released in 1991 by Walt Disney. Now streaming on VUDU/Prime/Disney+.

articles.text: Review by Chris Honoré Captain America: The First Avenger is, at least initially, set in New York City. The year is 1942. Steve Rogers (Chris Evans) and his best friend, Sgt. Bucky Barnes (Sebastian Stan), are downtown attending a future technology exhibition, and happen to pass a military recruitment station. War is in the air, Bucky is about to ship out for Europe, and countless men are enlisting, with the exception of Steve, who suffers from asthma and weighs in at some 98 pounds. It’s not for trying that he’s not in uniform. To his chagrin he’s been rejected multiple times. As it happens, also attending the exhibition is Dr. Abraham Erskine (Stanley Rucci), a brilliant inventor and genetic scientist, working on a special “super soldier” experiment for the Strategic Scientific Reserve. The project is under the command of Col. Chester Phillips (Tommy Lee Jones). Dr. Erskine happens to overhear a conversation of regret between Bucky and Steve. Looking at the scrawny Steve , he Steve might be perfect for his special serum and what are referred to as “vita rays.” Pulling a few strings with Col. Phillips, the scientist manages to get Steve into the program. Ever hopeful, willing to try anything to enlist, he agrees. Stretched out on a table, machinery begins to hum and spark, the serum/vita rays are administered, and to his surprise, Steve emerges much taller, more muscular, with an ability to now run at a tremendous speed. In other words, he has been indeed transformed into a super soldier. Amazing at the result, the army decides to dress him in stars and striped tights, hood, provide him with a shield and send him cross-country to advertise for war bonds using the name Captain America. The best part of Captain America is the transformation of weakling Steve Rogers into his alter ego. He’s now a square-jawed, humble, even shy superhero who soon is sent out to fight for truth, justice, and the American way. Soon he confronts his uber-nemesis and Nazi provocateur, the villainous, megalomaniac Red Skull (Hugo Weaving) and his army of thugs called Hydra, all ensconced in Red Skull’s alpine forest retreat where he is conducting his own experiment: a blue-cube that will enable him to take over the world. The story is a big, bold, razzle-dazzle adventure, and has plenty of action, chase scenes, shootouts, a submarine, aircraft, and even a fight on top of a Nazi blimp, all leading to a spectacular showdown between Captain America and Red Skull. And there’s even a touch of romance between MI 16 Brit spy, Peggy Carter (Hayley Atwell), who has been assigned to the Strategic Reserve. Kids will love this origin film, one that will soon be followed by The Avengers, introducing lots of superheroes. Stay tuned. Captain America: The First Avenger. Directed by Joe Johnson. Starring Chris Evans, Hayley Atwell, and Hugo Weaving. 2 hrs., 4 min. Rated PG. Released in 2011. Now Streaming on VUDY/Prime/Disney+.

articles.text: What makes piano music “classical?” Piedmont Adult School is offering a new course, Classical Piano Appreciation, for anyone interested in expanding their knowledge of this important genre. Students will learn what elements define classical music and how the piano has evolved to remain relevant in the 300 years since invention. They will become familiar with the most famous composers and pianists and their best-known works, as well as the misconceptions and misunderstandings about classical piano music. The class will be discussion-based and responsive to specific student interests. Piano experience is welcome but not required. Instructor Daniel Finnamore has taught piano lessons for 47 years, beginning with the Oakland Conservatory, located in the historic Sherman and Clay Building in downtown Oakland. Piedmonters may know Daniel Finnamore, the instructor of the new course Classical Piano Appreciation, from his performance at the Piedmont Center for the Arts in 2014. He made his public solo debut at age 20. His San Francisco debut, a benefit concert for the Liszt Society, was favorably reviewed by future Time magazine music critic Michael Walsh. Daniel has made five CDs of piano music by Brahms, Debussy, Liszt and various classical Spanish composers. He performed a concert at the Piedmont Center for the Arts in December 2014.

articles.text: The Piedmont Recreation Depar tment’s Walking on Wednesdays group had a large turnout of 32 walkers and one K-9 best friend. They admitted that they find the local real estate market pretty interesting. There are currently a number of beautiful homes for sale in Piedmont. Eight homes with listing prices ranging from $2,450,000 to $18,500,000 could be walked in a loop that would take the group to the top of Glen Alpine Road, a great street that the walkers hadn’t been to this year. There was some elevation gain, but anyone not wanting to climb to the top could peel off at Hampton Park. There was also some Piedmont history associated with this walk. The walkers headed off for the first house at 21 King Avenue by going up Highland Avenue to Sheridan and Lincoln Avenues, and turning down King. About midway down the street they spotted a Sold sign. It. The home was built in 1925, and. The group had fun making guesses on this 4 bedroom/3 bath, 3760 square foot home’s listing price, which was $3,250,000. The group retraced its steps back to Lincoln and went up to Sea View Avenue. Turning right, they came to 70 Sea View. a 5 bedroom/7 bath, 7,162 square foot home designed by Claude B. Barton and built in 1923 on roughly 1 acre. The group also made their guesses on the listing price, which is $10,800,000. Continuing on Sea View they passed more beautiful homes, including two having construction work done. The walkers then turned up Hampton Road to view the house at 395 Hampton, known historically as Hampton House. It is a 1928 Albert Farr-designed, 8 bedroom/9 bath, 11,150 square foot mansion on .93 acres and has an ADU next door at 1 Glen Alpine Road. At $18,500,000, this was the walking tour’s highest listed priced home and a spot worthy of the attached group photo. At the top of Glen Alpine was another Albert Farr mansion, 75 Glen Alpine. It is a 5 bedroom/8 bath, 11,938 square foot, French revival chateau built in 1926 on 1.62 acres, and listed for $11,500,000. It’s an impressive home, sitting at the top of this impressive street. Will Adams, who is a planner, urban designer, and architect, and writes regular “Walking Piedmont” articles in the Post, made some comments on Farr’s exterior design. In 1914 James Tyson, a wealthy lumber and shipping businessman, purchased 30 acres here to build his estate, which he named “Oakmont.” The property is house is now 70 Sotelo, but the Oakmont mansion was demolished in 1964. He also built a carriage house as a garage and servant quarters where he and his wife could live temporarily while supervising the construction of their new home, which was completed in 1916. This carriage house is the lovely home at 45 Glen Alpine that the walkers passed on the way up the hill. To the right of 75 Glen Alpine are Tyson’s original, two sandstone pillars which marked the entrance to the long driveway to Tyson’s now-gone mansion. The walkers descended on Sotelo Avenue, which forms half of the loop road above Tyson Lake, another Tyson creation. After he built Oakmont he dammed a small creek that ran through his property and created this reservoir, which is now owned and managed by a neighborhood association. The house at 7 Sotelo provided another surprise. This is a 3 bedroom/3 bath, 2,945 square foot home built in 1948. It was the first time this home was on the market, as it was built for the great grandparents of the sellers. At a listing price of “only” $2,750,000, it seemed like a bargain to the walkers. Everyone had enjoyed the walking tour to these beautiful homes, but it was time to return to the center of town. The Walking on Wednesdays group meets every Wednesday at the Exedra (Highland & Magnolia Avenues) at 10:30 a.m. Everyone is invited to join the group and there is no charge. pages.text: Wednesday, August 31, 2022 25 Walking on Wednesday Wednesday Walkers take a tour of Piedmont mansions The Piedmont Recreation Depar tment’s Walking on Wednesdays group had a large turnout of 32 walkers and one K-9 best friend. They admitted that they find the local real estate market pretty interesting. There are currently a number of beautiful homes for sale in Piedmont. Eight homes with listing prices ranging from $2,450,000 to $18,500,000 could be walked in a loop that would take the group to the top of Glen Alpine Road, a great street that the walkers hadn’t been to this year. There was some elevation gain, but anyone not wanting to climb to the top could peel off at Hampton Park. There was also some Piedmont history associated with this walk. The walkers headed off for the first house at 21 King Avenue by going up Highland Avenue to Sheridan and Lincoln Avenues, and turning down King. About midway down the street they spotted a Sold sign. It. The home was built in 1925, and. The group had fun making guesses on this 4 bedroom/3 bath, 3760 square foot home’s listing price, which was $3,250,000. The group retraced its steps back to Lincoln and went up to Sea View Avenue. Turning right, they came to 70 Sea View. a 5 bedroom/7 bath, 7,162 square foot home designed by Claude B. Barton and built in 1923 on roughly 1 acre. The group also made their guesses on the listing price, which is $10,800,000. Continuing on Sea View they passed more beautiful homes, including two having construction work done. The walkers then turned up Hampton Road to view the house at 395 Hampton, known historically as Hampton House. It is a 1928 Albert Farr-designed, 8 bedroom/9 bath, 11,150 square foot mansion on .93 acres and has an ADU next door at 1 Glen Alpine Road. At $18,500,000, this was the walking tour’s highest listed priced home and a spot worthy of the attached group photo. At the top of Glen Alpine was another Albert Farr mansion, 75 Glen Alpine. It is a 5 bedroom/8 bath, 11,938 square foot, French revival chateau built in 1926 on 1.62 acres, and listed for $11,500,000. It’s an impressive home, sitting at the top of this impressive street. Will Adams, who is a planner, urban designer, and architect, and writes regular “Walking Piedmont” articles in the Post, made some comments on Farr’s exterior design. In 1914 James Tyson, a wealthy lumber and shipping businessman, purchased 30 acres here to build his estate, which he named “Oakmont.” The property is house is now 70 Sotelo, but the Oakmont mansion was demolished in 1964. He also built a carriage house as a garage and servant quarters where he and his wife could live temporarily while supervising the construction of their new home, which was completed in 1916. This carriage house is the lovely home at 45 Glen Alpine that the walkers passed on the way up the hill. To the right of 75 Glen Alpine are Tyson’s original, two sandstone pillars which marked the entrance to the long driveway to Tyson’s now-gone mansion. The walkers descended on Sotelo Avenue, which forms half of the loop road above Tyson Lake, another Tyson creation. After he built Oakmont he dammed a small creek that ran through his property and created this reservoir, which is now owned and managed by a neighborhood association. The house at 7 Sotelo provided another surprise. This is a 3 bedroom/3 bath, 2,945 square foot home built in 1948. It was the first time this home was on the market, as it was built for the great grandparents of the sellers. At a listing price of “only” $2,750,000, it seemed like a bargain to the walkers. Everyone had enjoyed the walking tour to these beautiful homes, but it was time to return to the center of town. The Walking on Wednesdays group meets every Wednesday at the Exedra (Highland & Magnolia Avenues) at 10:30 a.m. Everyone is invited to join the group and there is no charge. New walkers and their friendly K-9 best friends are especially welcome. Registration with the Piedmont Recreation Department is required at https://tinyurl. com/3ethkehu. articles.text: Your son and his partner are having a baby. You’re very excited and can’t wait to hear whether it’s a boy or a girl. They must be dying to know, too, so you’re certain that they will take advantage of the earliest medical tests available to determine the baby’s sex. Of course, they will. Wait, what? Your son tells you that he and his partner have chosen not to learn the sex of the baby before birth. OK, that’s fine. They just like surprises, right? It will be exciting to learn when the baby is delivered. Wrong again. You’re stunned to learn that the expectant parents will not be sharing the baby’s sex before birth, nor will they announce this bit of information after the baby arrives. Like a growing group of parents, they believe that assigning sex at birth is wrong, that every child should be able to discover their own gender identity for themselves, and that they should be allowed to express that identity freely in any way that they choose. What is meant by gender identity? For an excellent explanation of this term and others, please visit www.thinkorblue.com. assigned by a medical professional at a baby’s birth depending on the visual inspection of the newborn’s genitals. Gender identity is often defined as how a person perceives their own gender – whether they feel that they are male or female. This is something that a person learns about themselves over time and is not something that can be determined by others. Today’s parents are raising families in a world that in many ways bears no resemblance to the one in which you raised your children. Terms such as gay and lesbian may be familiar to you, while genderqueer, cis & trans, transgender, transmasculine, transfeminine, gender non-conforming, non-binary, gender-neutral, gender-fluid, etc., may not be. Yet these are likely to be common words in your children’s vocabulary, and the sooner you learn their accurate definitions, the better. Almost every family will have a loved one who identifies outside the stereotypical gender norms. If you have not yet experienced this in your family, you probably will one day. As you watch your adult children raising their families, keep in mind that it’s their turn. How you respond to your children and your grandchildren’s perspectives and lived experiences around the issue of gender identity is no different than anything else. Be open to what your loved ones feel and believe, no matter how much it may differ from your own beliefs. Lovingly support the free expression of their inner selves and think before assuming stereotypical gender roles for them. Be the first one to let them know they are loved just the way they are. The communities in which we live may take a long time to bring equity and inclusion to all persons. But you can begin this process of loving acceptance at home even before your grandchild is born. articles.text: A professional caregiver can become like a member of the family over time as they provide meaningful home care services when some are at their most vulnerable. However, they likely start out as a stranger to not only the person who is receiving care but also that person’s family. Here are five ways to break the ice and get to know your caregiver better so that caregiving becomes familiar and builds a stronger relationship. 1. Ask them how they became a caregiver. Often people get into the caregiving business after caring for a loved one at one home and seeing the profound impact of one-on-one care for someone who is recovering from a surgery, living with the symptoms of a chronic condition, or just adjusting to changing abilities with age. This might spark a conversation about different jobs you had in life. The key to building any lasting relationship is sharing, so if they seem shy, take the first step and talk about any caregiving experiences of your own. 2. Find out about their skills. Feel free to ask if they have done any meal preparation before if that’s something you or your loved one might need. Or ask if they have experience in caring for someone with a specific condition such as dementia, Parkinson’s Disease, diabetes, or something else. Caregivers may attend to many clients for short visits or work with just one client each day over a few years, so backgrounds and experience will vary. 3. Do they have hobbies? Everyone has something they are interested in outside of what they get paid to do, even if it’s a favorite TV show they watch regularly or talking with a relative at a predictable day and time. Care can be a two-way street with one person receiving and one person giving, but it is best when each person gets something out of it. Maybe you both love antique cars and go to a local museum or car show and share knowledge with one another. You may like the same TV show and watch it together or discuss the latest plot points and characters. These commonalities are a way to develop a bond outside of the tasks they are there to perform. 4. What information goes into the plan of care? A plan of care is a record of the tasks completed as well as details about someone’s preferences, so that their care can be customized as needs change. With a person-directed approach to care, it can be helpful to know how often this information is updated as it might inform how much or how little care is needed. Home care services evolve with needs, as well as preferences, so when the caregiver can be open about what notes they are sharing, it strengthens the back-andforth of this dynamic. 5. How do they handle challenges? In the best-case scenario home care is arranged in order to help prevent emergencies, but life happens. Making sure your caregiver has basic CPR and First Aid training can be a great help in the event of emergencies. If you or a loved one is living with a condition in which there are challenges with swallowing, for example, choking should be something that the caregiver should be trained to handle. Since each person is unique, this means that the caregivers have their own strengths and weaknesses when they come work. Good communication is key to most relationships. Caregiving is oftentimes a hybrid relationship spanning elements of professional and personal lives. And know that while sometimes a caregiver may be perfectly trained, they may not be a good fit. It’s okay to try someone else if the match is not there. Look for those soft traits, such as common interests or similar backgrounds, that can overcome differences in age or gender. Dear MacMama: When my neighbor set up my new iMac, he asked me if I would like to use iCloud to back up my files. What does that exactly mean? I think my contacts and calendars are on iCloud already. Lissa D., Oakland Dear Lissa: iCloud, Apple’s proprietary sync and storage system has been around in one form or another for several years. If you have more than one device, meaning your iMac, an iPhone and an iPad, making sure that your contacts and calendars are synced with iCloud makes things easier to keep all devices current. For instance, if you change an address on your phone, it is automatically changed on all other devices that have iCloud enabled. iCloud can also back up and synchronize your photos. In this case, your entire photo library is backed up in iCloud. Meaning that if your computer is lost, stolen, or just breaks, your photos are safe. To enable iCloud, you sign into your device with your Apple ID (which is your iCloud account) and password, and through the settings, check the items that you want synced. iCloud also has the possibility of storing and backing up your documents and the items on your desktop. When this is enabled, you can access the files in your documents folder and on your desktop from any device that is also signed into your iCloud account. This means that you can access your desktop files from your phone, iPad, or a web browser like Safari. You simply would go to icloud.com, sign in with your Apple/iCloud ID and password, and then access your photos, files, contacts, etc. Or on your phone or iPad, go to Files to find your stuff. In most cases, if you want to store and back up most of the items on your computer on iCloud, you would have to increase the free storage amount that you get when you have an Apple ID, which is 5 GB. So, then you would sign up for what is called iCloud plus to increase the storage. Offered first in 2017, the costs for extra storage are quite reasonable, $.99 a month for up to 50 GB, and $2.99 a month for up to 200 GB. You can even get 2 TB for $9.99. And with a good back up plan, meaning a time machine back up, this cloud backup gives you extra safety and redundancy. I know sometimes clients are worried about the safety of cloud back up, but Apple uses industry standard methods for securing data in iCloud. When they first came out with the ability to back up photos and data, there were definitely a few bumps in the road, but I feel good enough about it to do it with my own data. Of course, it can be daunting to incorporate a new system of backing up to the cloud, but so much is stored in the cloud by our banks, Social Security the IRS, and other organizations that require security. And in our area where earthquakes are reality, and fires are a danger, cloud back up just makes sense. Google Drive, Dropbox, and Microsoft One Drive are other examples of cloud storage and back up possibilities. In reality I use iCloud, Dropbox and Google Drive seamlessly. Drop box in google drive are excellent, but no replacement for iCloud which offers benefits not available on the other services, like syncing all of your Apple devices. On a beautiful, sunny June day 16 members of the Piedmont Seniors group visited the Charles Schultz Museum and the Luther Burbank Home & Gardens in Santa Rosa. This year is memorable: it marks 100 years since the birth of Charles Schultz, aka “Sparky”, the cartoonist of the comic strip Peanuts. He was born in Minnesota in 1922 and knew from an early age that he wanted to draw “funny pictures”. His comic strips have appeared in over 2600 newspapers worldwide and his books have been translated into 25 languages. Schultz wanted to name his strips “L’ll folks” but there was concern about possible copyright infringement with a cartoon called Little Folks by Tack Knight published in the 1930s. Schulz suggested Charlie Brown or Good Ol’ Charlie Brown, but the syndicate decided upon Peanuts. The name “Peanuts” was likely chosen because it was a well-known term for children at the time, popularized by the live television program “Howdy Doody Show” with an audience section for children called “the Peanut Gallery”. The Schultz Museum is very modern and inviting. The museum even has a theatre, where one can look at the posted schedule on the wall and then choose to watch films which rotate on a regular basis. The Piedmont Seniors were fortunate to have a wonderful and knowledgeable docent who had a wealth of information about Schultz and his endeavors. Schultz most identified with Charlie, a boy who never caught or kicked the football, but kept trying. Schultz created over 70 distinct characters in the Peanuts strip. Schultz most likely had a beloved blanket, much like Linus, and, let’s face it, who doesn’t know someone like the bossy Lucy? The characters are based upon Schultz’s own experiences. He once said, “almost all of the characters are mine, including the wishy-washiness of Charles and the sarcasm of Lucy”. The beauty of the comic strip is that it is timeless and appeals to people of all age. When the tour was over, the group headed across the street to the Warm Puppy Café for reserved box lunches, in a relaxed outdoor setting. There is a large, inviting gift shop also on the property with something for everybody. You can even see Snoopy’s World War One Sopwith Camel airplane hanging from the store’s ceiling as Snoopy pretends his doghouse is the airplane used to fight the Red Baron. The last stop before returning home was a visit to Luther Burbank’s Home and Gardens, also in Santa Rosa. Just a short distance from the Schultz Museum, the Burbank museum is a step back in time. It is a city park containing the gardens, greenhouse, home and grave of one of the most famous American horticulturists. Visitors can see how Burbank lived from 1906 until his death in 1926. Burbank was so famous that Arbor Day is celebrated on March 7 in honor of his birthday. He became an early media celebrity as he welcomed visitors from around the world to his home and gardens. Burbank introduced hundreds of new plant varieties, including his famous spineless cactus. The trip is certainly worth the 1-hour drive to see all of Burbank’s accomplishments. Tours are available for his house and gardens where o can learn about horticulture as well as his gardening experiments with fruit trees as well as plants. The Piedmont Seniors had a wonderful day learning about two famous people who contributed so much to the history of Sonoma County. The Doctor is In: Mona Jamieson and Penny Robb. Burbank was so famous that Arbor Day is celebrated on March 7 in honor of his birthday. He became an early media celebrity as he welcomed visitors from around the world to his home and gardens.
